title: King Haakon Refuses the German Demands
text:
Early on April 9, 1940, Germany invaded Norway. The royal family, the government and members of parliament escaped from Oslo by train just ahead of the German forces, heading north into the interior. That same day the Norwegian fascist Vidkun Quisling declared himself prime minister on the radio.

On April 10 the German envoy, Curt Brauer, met King Haakon VII at Elverum and demanded that he appoint a government headed by Quisling. Haakon's powers as a constitutional monarch were limited, and he said he could not answer without consulting his ministers.

That evening he met the cabinet at Nybergsund. He told them that he could not appoint Quisling, a man he knew had no support among the people, and that if the government decided to accept the German demands, he would abdicate rather than be part of it. The ministers, who had been uncertain, unanimously backed him. The answer to Germany was no.

The next day German bombers attacked Nybergsund, and the king and crown prince sheltered in the snowy woods. After two months of fighting, Haakon and the government left for Britain in June 1940 and led the resistance from exile. He returned to Norway on June 7, 1945.
lesson: Even when your formal power is small, refusing to lend your name to injustice can stiffen everyone around you.
people: Haakon VII of Norway, Curt Brauer, Vidkun Quisling
source: Norwegian government records; contemporary accounts and later memoirs of ministers present
